Spoiler free review by me: So I'll start off by saying I really wasn't expecting much from this movie. I watched the production problems go down and it really made me lose hope that this will be any good, plus it's Antman who cares about him. So coming out of this I have to say I'm pleasantly surprised with how much I enjoyed this movie. Not saying it was absolutely amazing but it was entertaining and some parts are going to stick with me.

So let's start with the acting and characters. I thought everyone in the film fit their role perfectly, especially Michael Douglas as Hank Pym. Douglas to me really stole the whole show and really showed what he can do. Paul Rudd was very funny which is to be expected so not anything surprising there. I fell like Evangeline Lilly was kind of underused in this movie to be perfectly honest. She starts off as just kind of a character that has to be there and really doesn't turn into a good character until the last half of the movie. So now onto Corey Stoll as Darren Cross. The most common problem with marvel movies is the villain and this is the case in every villain they've put on screen except Loki. This film is no different in that Darren Cross is just another generic evil guy trying to make money off some type of weapon, you know the thing pretty much every marvel villain has done. The acting by Stoll was solid throughout but he really suffered from standard boring marvel villain syndrome. Michael Peña was really funny and his chemistry with Rudd and really the rest of the heist crew was really good. That's all I can really say about him.

The story itself was pretty much what you'd expect and you see pretty much everything coming before it happens. It gets a little heavy handed in the foreshadowing so nothing that happens is really that big of a surprise for anyone. Action is what we all really want to see out of a superhero film and this movie really delivers on that. Every fight sequence was incredibly well shot and actually very coherent even with the mass amounts of switching between sizes. The shrinking scenes were actually incredibly well done and I loved the way they showed them off, especially when he's first learning how to use the suit. And of course we have to talk about the comedy. Paul Rudd as Scott Lang may be one of the funniest marvel characters to come along besides Pratt's Star Lord. I really feel like none of his lines fell flat, they were all incredibly well delivered and made me laugh almost every time he opened his mouth.

So basic conclusion is this movie is a lot of fun but predictable. If you want to go to the movies just to have a good time and enjoy yourself this is the movie to go see. Like a said the villain was bland which is a big downer for me but it pretty much makes up for in Scott Lang's character. Overall I'd give this movie a 7-8/10. It would Defiantly be in the top half of marvel movies and I can't wait to see what they are going to do with this in the future.

Yes, the cesarean rate has increased considerably since the mid 1990s, by 50%. In recent years, it has actually leveled off and perhaps begun to decrease. It isn't clear why it has increased so much. Pregnant women today are, on average, older and heavier than in the past, both of which increase the likelihood of a cesarean, but cesarean rates have increased even in low risk women. There's been a lot of research into why the rate has increased, and a push from public health and professional organizations to figure out how to safely lower the rate.

A likely contributor is the fear of malpractice suits. OB is a high risk specialization, for the physician. Chances are they will get sued at least once in their career. Especially if baby ends up brain injured, awards tend to be high, and thus their insurance premiums are high. Moreover, no one wants to be faced with a negative outcomes. So there's a push to err on the side of intervention. The consequences of not doing a cesarean that was necessary are immediate and dramatic, while many of the risks of cesarean tend to be downstream, such as increased risk in subsequent pregnancies. And even serious morbidity in the mother, one of the biggest risks of cesarean, does not garner the sympathy or monetary awards that a damaged baby does.

There's real risk to being hesitant to do a cesarean, too, which is why research to determine when cesarean improves outcomes and when it doesn't is so very important, although very difficult to do.

In 1985, Edwards represented a five-year-old child born with cerebral palsy – a child whose mother's doctor did not choose to perform an immediate Caesarean delivery when a fetal monitor showed she was in distress. Winning this case established the North Carolina precedent of physician and hospital liability for failing to determine if the patient understood the risks of a particular procedure.
